_meta.topicName: Biochemical Pathways: Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration

items.title: I can state the purpose of photosynthesis
items.what: Photosynthesis is an anabolic reaction in which light energy is used to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen inside the chloroplast.
items.why: Knowing the purpose distinguishes photosynthesis from cellular respiration and establishes why autotrophs can sustain themselves without consuming other organisms.
items.example: A spinach plant uses light energy, CO2 from the air and H2O from the soil to produce glucose for growth and O2 as a waste product.

subtopic.name: Photosynthesis
subtopic.what: Covers the purpose of photosynthesis, the structure of the chloroplast, and the inputs, outputs and locations of the light dependent and light independent stages in C3 plants. Includes the roles of key molecules such as Rubisco, ATP synthase, NADP+ and RuBP.
subtopic.why: Photosynthesis is the foundation of almost all food chains on Earth and is a core example of how biochemical pathways convert one form of energy to another. Understanding its stages and molecular components is essential for VCE Biology assessment and for making sense of how organisms regulate energy.

items.title: I can explain the general function of the chloroplast
items.what: The chloroplast is the organelle in plant and algal cells where photosynthesis occurs. It contains chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes and enzymes in the stroma that carry out the two stages of photosynthesis.
items.why: Linking organelle structure to function is a recurring assessment skill. Understanding why the chloroplast is the site of photosynthesis requires knowing what each internal region does.
items.example: Chlorophyll is embedded in the thylakoid membranes of the grana, so light energy is captured there during the light dependent stage.

items.title: I can draw and label a chloroplast and recall the function of its key structures
items.what: A chloroplast has an outer membrane, inner membrane, grana (stacks of thylakoid membranes), stroma, ribosomes, DNA and starch granules. Each structure has a specific role in photosynthesis.
items.why: Labelled diagrams are frequently assessed in VCE Biology. Knowing the function of each structure allows you to connect structure to the stages of photosynthesis.
items.example: The stroma surrounds the grana and is the site of the light independent stage (Calvin Cycle), so it contains many ribosomes to produce the enzymes needed for those reactions.

items.title: I can state the word equation and balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis
items.what: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → oxygen + glucose (requires light energy and chlorophyll). Balanced equation: 6CO2 + 12H2O → 6O2 + 6H2O + C6H12O6, or simplified: 6CO2 + 6H2O → 6O2 + C6H12O6.
items.why: The equation summarises all inputs and outputs of photosynthesis. In assessments, the arrow must include 'light energy' and 'chlorophyll' to be awarded marks.
items.example: If a question asks for the equation for photosynthesis, writing 'carbon dioxide + water → oxygen + glucose' without 'light energy' and 'chlorophyll' on the arrow will not receive full marks.

items.title: I can summarise the inputs, outputs and location of the two stages of photosynthesis in C3 plants
items.what: The light dependent stage occurs on the thylakoid membranes and uses light energy and water to produce ATP, NADPH and O2. The light independent stage (Calvin Cycle) occurs in the stroma and uses CO2, ATP and NADPH to produce glucose and regenerate RuBP.
items.why: Tabulating inputs, outputs and locations is a direct Study Design requirement and a common exam question format. Confusing the two stages is a frequent student error.
items.example: In a table: Light dependent stage — inputs: light energy, H2O; outputs: ATP, NADPH, O2; location: thylakoid membranes.

items.title: I can outline what occurs during the light dependent and light independent stages of photosynthesis
items.what: In the light dependent stage, chlorophyll absorbs light energy, water is split by photolysis producing O2, H+ and electrons, ATP is synthesised by ATP synthase and NADP+ is reduced to NADPH. In the light independent stage, RuBP combines with CO2 (via Rubisco) to form PGA, which is converted to PGAL using ATP and NADPH, then PGAL forms glucose and regenerates RuBP.
items.why: Describing both stages in sequence shows understanding of how the two stages depend on each other, which is tested in extended response questions.
items.example: The ATP and NADPH produced in the light dependent stage are transported to the stroma and used to drive the reactions of the Calvin Cycle in the light independent stage.

items.title: I can describe the role of Rubisco and ATP synthase in photosynthesis
items.what: Rubisco (RuBP carboxylase) is the enzyme that catalyses the fixation of CO2 to RuBP in the Calvin Cycle, producing PGA. ATP synthase is an enzyme embedded in the thylakoid membrane that catalyses the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using energy from electron flow.
items.why: Both enzymes are named in the Study Design and are commonly used in exam questions to test understanding of specific molecular roles within a broader pathway.
items.example: If Rubisco is inhibited, CO2 cannot be fixed to RuBP and no PGA is produced, so the Calvin Cycle stops and glucose cannot be made.

items.title: I can list the factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis
items.what: The four factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis are light availability, water availability, temperature and carbon dioxide concentration. Each is a limiting factor when in short supply.
items.why: Listing these factors is the starting point for deeper explanation questions. A limiting factor is any factor that slows the rate of photosynthesis when insufficient.
items.example: In a greenhouse at night with artificial lights, light is no longer limiting, but CO2 concentration may become the factor that limits the rate of photosynthesis.

subtopic.name: Factors Affecting the Rate of Photosynthesis
subtopic.what: Covers the four factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis (light availability, water availability, temperature and CO2 concentration), the concept of a limiting factor, photorespiration and the adaptations of C3, C4 and CAM plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding how external conditions alter photosynthetic rate requires integrating enzyme theory with the specific biochemistry of photosynthesis. These concepts also connect directly to agricultural applications and are a source of multi-part exam questions.

items.title: I can explain why and how each factor affects the rate of photosynthesis
items.what: Light intensity increases reaction rate up to a plateau where chloroplasts are working at maximum capacity. Temperature affects enzyme activity, increasing rate to the optimum then decreasing as enzymes denature. CO2 concentration increases rate until enzyme active sites are saturated. Water stress causes stomata to close, limiting CO2 entry and reducing photosynthesis.
items.why: Examiners regularly ask students to explain the mechanism behind a graph or trend. Knowing the enzyme-based reason for each pattern is required for full marks.
items.example: At temperatures above the optimum, Rubisco denatures and its active site changes shape, so CO2 can no longer bind and carbon fixation stops, causing the rate of photosynthesis to fall sharply.

subtopic.name: Factors Affecting the Rate of Photosynthesis
subtopic.what: Covers the four factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis (light availability, water availability, temperature and CO2 concentration), the concept of a limiting factor, photorespiration and the adaptations of C3, C4 and CAM plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding how external conditions alter photosynthetic rate requires integrating enzyme theory with the specific biochemistry of photosynthesis. These concepts also connect directly to agricultural applications and are a source of multi-part exam questions.

items.title: I can describe the role of Rubisco in maximising photosynthetic efficiency and define photorespiration
items.what: Rubisco normally fixes CO2 to RuBP to begin the Calvin Cycle. However, when O2 concentration is high (e.g. when stomata are closed), Rubisco binds O2 instead of CO2, initiating photorespiration. Photorespiration is an inefficient process that produces no glucose and wastes energy, reducing photosynthetic efficiency by approximately 25% in C3 plants.
items.why: Photorespiration is a key reason why C3 plants are less efficient in hot, dry conditions and is the basis for understanding why C4 and CAM adaptations are advantageous.
items.example: On a hot dry day, a wheat plant closes its stomata to conserve water. O2 builds up inside the leaf. Rubisco begins binding O2 instead of CO2, and photorespiration occurs, wasting energy and producing no glucose.

subtopic.name: Factors Affecting the Rate of Photosynthesis
subtopic.what: Covers the four factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis (light availability, water availability, temperature and CO2 concentration), the concept of a limiting factor, photorespiration and the adaptations of C3, C4 and CAM plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding how external conditions alter photosynthetic rate requires integrating enzyme theory with the specific biochemistry of photosynthesis. These concepts also connect directly to agricultural applications and are a source of multi-part exam questions.

items.title: I can summarise the adaptations of C3, C4 and CAM plants that maximise photosynthetic efficiency
items.what: C3 plants (e.g. wheat, rice) fix CO2 directly in the mesophyll using Rubisco but are vulnerable to photorespiration. C4 plants (e.g. maize, sugar cane) fix CO2 as a 4C compound in the mesophyll and release it in low-O2 bundle sheath cells for the Calvin Cycle, reducing photorespiration. CAM plants (e.g. cacti, pineapple) open stomata only at night to fix CO2 as a 4C compound, releasing it during the day when stomata are closed.
items.why: The contrast between C3, C4 and CAM plants is a direct Study Design dot point and often appears as a table-completion or extended response question in exams.
items.example: A CAM plant such as a cactus in a desert opens its stomata at night to take in CO2 and stores it as a 4C compound. During the hot day, stomata remain closed to prevent water loss, and the stored CO2 is released for use in the Calvin Cycle.

subtopic.what: Covers the four factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis (light availability, water availability, temperature and CO2 concentration), the concept of a limiting factor, photorespiration and the adaptations of C3, C4 and CAM plants.
subtopic.why: Understanding how external conditions alter photosynthetic rate requires integrating enzyme theory with the specific biochemistry of photosynthesis. These concepts also connect directly to agricultural applications and are a source of multi-part exam questions.

items.title: I can draw, recognise and interpret graphical representations of rates of photosynthesis
items.what: Rate of photosynthesis graphs typically show an initial increase with increasing light, CO2 or temperature, followed by a plateau (for light and CO2) or a sharp drop after the optimum (for temperature). Interpreting these graphs requires linking the shape of the curve to enzyme or chloroplast behaviour.
items.why: Graph interpretation is a core scientific skill assessed in both SACs and the external exam. Being able to read off data points and explain the trend using biological reasoning is expected.
items.example: In a graph showing rate of photosynthesis vs light intensity, the flat section of the curve indicates that light is no longer the limiting factor and another factor, such as CO2 concentration or chloroplast capacity, is now limiting the rate.

items.title: I can state the purpose of cellular respiration
items.what: Cellular respiration is a series of biochemical reactions in which glucose is broken down to produce ATP, the cell's primary energy currency. It occurs in all living cells and can proceed with oxygen (aerobic) or without it (anaerobic).
items.why: Distinguishing between the purpose of cellular respiration (making ATP) and the purpose of photosynthesis (making glucose) is a common point of confusion assessed in exams.
items.example: Muscle cells during exercise carry out aerobic cellular respiration to produce the ATP needed to power muscle contraction.

subtopic.name: Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can explain the function of the mitochondria
items.what: The mitochondrion is the site of the Krebs Cycle (in the matrix) and the electron transport chain (on the cristae of the inner membrane). It converts the chemical energy in pyruvate into ATP through these two stages of aerobic cellular respiration.
items.why: The mitochondrion is central to aerobic respiration and its structural features directly explain its function. This connection between structure and function is regularly assessed.
items.example: Cells that perform a lot of active transport, such as intestinal epithelial cells, contain large numbers of mitochondria because they require large amounts of ATP.

subtopic.name: Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can draw and label a mitochondrion and recall the function of its key structures
items.what: A mitochondrion has an outer membrane, inner membrane, cristae (folds of the inner membrane), matrix, ribosomes and DNA. The cristae increase surface area for the electron transport chain; the matrix contains enzymes for the Krebs Cycle.
items.why: Like the chloroplast, the mitochondrion is a high-priority diagram in VCE Biology. Labelling it correctly and linking each structure to a function is expected in assessment.
items.example: A mitochondrion with many deep cristae has a greater surface area for the electron transport chain, so more ATP can be produced per unit time compared to a mitochondrion with fewer cristae.

subtopic.name: Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can demonstrate an understanding of the energy shuttle and uses of ATP
items.what: ATP acts as an energy shuttle by storing energy in a high-energy bond between its second and third phosphate groups. When that bond is broken (ATP → ADP + Pi), energy is released for cellular processes. Energy is stored again when ADP is phosphorylated back to ATP.
items.why: The ATP-ADP cycle underpins every energy-requiring process in the cell. Understanding it is required for explaining how energy is transferred between the stages of cellular respiration and for answering questions about endergonic and exergonic reactions.
items.example: When a nerve cell fires an impulse, ATP is hydrolysed to ADP + Pi, releasing energy to power the sodium-potassium pump. The ADP is then recharged to ATP using energy from cellular respiration.

subtopic.name: Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can tabulate the inputs, outputs, location and ATP yield of each stage of aerobic cellular respiration
items.what: Glycolysis: cytosol, inputs glucose, outputs 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP + 2 NADH. Krebs Cycle: matrix, inputs 2 acetyl CoA + NAD+ + FAD+, outputs CO2 + 2 ATP + NADH + FADH2. Electron transport chain: cristae, inputs NADH + FADH2 + O2, outputs H2O + 26 or 28 ATP.
items.why: Tabulating all three stages with correct inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields is a direct Study Design requirement and a very common exam question format.
items.example: In a table: Krebs Cycle — location: matrix of mitochondrion; inputs: acetyl CoA, NAD+, FAD+; outputs: CO2, NADH, FADH2; ATP yield: 2 per glucose.

subtopic.name: Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can outline what occurs during glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain
items.what: Glycolysis splits one glucose (6C) into two pyruvate (3C) molecules in the cytosol, producing 2 ATP and 2 NADH. The Krebs Cycle converts pyruvate (via acetyl CoA) in the matrix, releasing CO2 and producing NADH, FADH2 and 2 ATP. The electron transport chain uses H+ ions from NADH and FADH2 to drive ATP synthase on the cristae, producing up to 28 ATP and water.
items.why: Describing what occurs at each stage, rather than just listing inputs and outputs, is required for extended response questions and multi-mark explanations.
items.example: During the electron transport chain, electrons from NADH and FADH2 pass through a series of protein complexes on the cristae. The energy released pumps H+ across the membrane, and as H+ flow back through ATP synthase, ATP is produced. At the end of the chain, H+ and electrons combine with O2 to form water.

subtopic.name: Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can state the word equation and balanced chemical equation for aerobic cellular respiration
items.what: Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP). Balanced equation: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + 30 or 32 ATP.
items.why: The overall equation for cellular respiration summarises all reactants and products and is frequently required in both short-answer and multiple-choice questions.
items.example: If a question asks what the products of aerobic cellular respiration are, the answer is carbon dioxide, water and ATP — not just energy, which is too vague for a biology response.

subtopic.name: Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can tabulate the inputs, outputs, location and difference in products of anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts
items.what: All anaerobic fermentation begins with glycolysis (cytosol, glucose → 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP). In animals: pyruvate is converted to lactic acid in the cytosol. In plants and yeast: pyruvate is converted to ethanol and CO2 in the cytosol. Both pathways restore NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.
items.why: The difference in products between animal and yeast/plant fermentation is a specific Study Design requirement. It is regularly tested in short-answer format.
items.example: During intense sprint exercise, human muscle cells run short of oxygen and switch to lactic acid fermentation, producing lactic acid and 2 ATP per glucose. Yeast in bread dough under the same anaerobic conditions produces ethanol and CO2, causing the dough to rise.

subtopic.name: Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can state the word equation for anaerobic cellular respiration
items.what: For animals: glucose → lactic acid + 2 ATP. For plants and yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + 2 ATP.
items.why: Stating the correct word equation, including the correct products for the specific organism, is required for full marks in assessment. Mixing up lactic acid and ethanol is a common error.
items.example: If a question describes yeast fermenting sugar in a sealed container, the expected word equation is: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + 2 ATP.

subtopic.what: Covers the ATP-ADP energy shuttle, the structure of the mitochondrion, and the inputs, outputs, locations and ATP yields of glycolysis, the Krebs Cycle and the electron transport chain in aerobic respiration, as well as anaerobic fermentation in animals, plants and yeasts.
subtopic.why: Cellular respiration explains how all living cells extract usable energy from glucose. Understanding its stages is essential for explaining how organisms respond to changing oxygen availability and how ATP is produced to power all cellular processes.

items.title: I can list the factors that affect the rate of cellular respiration
items.what: The three factors that affect the rate of cellular respiration are temperature, glucose availability and oxygen concentration.
items.why: Listing these factors correctly without confusing them with factors affecting photosynthesis is the starting point for more detailed explanation questions.
items.example: A yeast population fermenting grape juice will respire faster as glucose concentration rises, up to the point where the enzymes involved are working at their maximum rate.

subtopic.name: Factors Affecting the Rate of Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the three factors that affect the rate of cellular respiration: temperature, glucose availability and oxygen concentration, and explains how each factor influences the rate through its effect on enzyme activity or substrate availability.
subtopic.why: These factors connect enzyme theory to cellular respiration directly, and are often assessed alongside graphs or experimental scenarios. Understanding them also explains the switch between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms.

items.title: I can explain why and how temperature affects the rate of cellular respiration
items.what: As temperature increases, kinetic energy of molecules increases, leading to more frequent successful collisions between substrates and enzyme active sites, so the rate of respiration rises. Above the optimum temperature, enzymes denature, their active site changes shape and substrates can no longer bind, causing the rate to fall sharply.
items.why: Temperature-rate graphs for cellular respiration follow the same enzyme-based pattern as those for photosynthesis. Being able to explain the shape of the curve using enzyme theory is essential for extended response marks.
items.example: At 37°C (human body temperature), the enzymes of cellular respiration operate near their optimum. If body temperature rises to 42°C during a high fever, enzyme denaturation begins and the rate of cellular respiration decreases.

subtopic.name: Factors Affecting the Rate of Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the three factors that affect the rate of cellular respiration: temperature, glucose availability and oxygen concentration, and explains how each factor influences the rate through its effect on enzyme activity or substrate availability.
subtopic.why: These factors connect enzyme theory to cellular respiration directly, and are often assessed alongside graphs or experimental scenarios. Understanding them also explains the switch between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms.

items.title: I can explain why and how glucose availability affects the rate of cellular respiration
items.what: Glucose is the primary substrate for cellular respiration. As glucose concentration increases, enzyme active sites are occupied more frequently and the rate of respiration rises. At very high glucose concentrations, all enzyme active sites are saturated and the rate plateaus.
items.why: Glucose availability links directly to the concept of substrate concentration from enzyme theory and explains real situations such as post-meal blood glucose spikes or athletic performance.
items.example: A graph of glucose concentration vs rate of cellular respiration shows a curve that rises steeply at low concentrations, then flattens into a plateau when enzyme active sites are fully saturated.

subtopic.name: Factors Affecting the Rate of Cellular Respiration
subtopic.what: Covers the three factors that affect the rate of cellular respiration: temperature, glucose availability and oxygen concentration, and explains how each factor influences the rate through its effect on enzyme activity or substrate availability.
subtopic.why: These factors connect enzyme theory to cellular respiration directly, and are often assessed alongside graphs or experimental scenarios. Understanding them also explains the switch between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms.

items.title: I can explain why and how oxygen concentration affects the rate of cellular respiration
items.what: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain. As oxygen concentration increases, the rate of the electron transport chain increases, producing more ATP. At very low oxygen levels, aerobic respiration slows and cells switch to anaerobic fermentation, producing only 2 ATP per glucose instead of 30 or 32.
items.why: Understanding the role of oxygen explains why cells switch between aerobic and anaerobic respiration and why aerobic respiration is far more efficient. This is assessed in scenarios involving exercise, sealed containers or low-oxygen environments.
items.example: When nitrogen gas is bubbled through a yeast solution to remove all oxygen, yeast switch to alcoholic fermentation, producing ethanol and CO2 and only 2 ATP per glucose. When oxygen is reintroduced, the rate of CO2 production increases significantly as aerobic respiration resumes.

subtopic.what: Covers the three factors that affect the rate of cellular respiration: temperature, glucose availability and oxygen concentration, and explains how each factor influences the rate through its effect on enzyme activity or substrate availability.
subtopic.why: These factors connect enzyme theory to cellular respiration directly, and are often assessed alongside graphs or experimental scenarios. Understanding them also explains the switch between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms.

items.title: I can define and explain the process involved in CRISPR-Cas9 technologies
items.what: CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene editing system derived from a bacterial immune response. Guide RNA (gRNA) is designed to match a target DNA sequence. The gRNA directs the Cas9 endonuclease enzyme to cut both strands of the DNA at a precise location. The cell's own DNA repair mechanisms then either delete, disrupt or insert a desired DNA sequence at the cut site.
items.why: CRISPR-Cas9 is named explicitly in the Study Design and its mechanism is assessed in both short-answer and extended response questions. Understanding the roles of guide RNA and Cas9 specifically is required.
items.example: To disable a gene that causes photorespiration in a crop plant, a researcher designs a guide RNA complementary to the target gene. The gRNA and Cas9 are injected into the plant cell, Cas9 cuts the DNA at that location and the cell's repair enzymes disrupt the gene so it is no longer expressed.

subtopic.name: Biotechnological Applications of Biochemical Pathways
subtopic.what: Covers the use of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to improve photosynthetic efficiency and crop yields, and the use of anaerobic fermentation of biomass to produce biofuels, including the distinction between first- and second-generation biofuels and the key steps in bioethanol production.
subtopic.why: These applications show how understanding biochemical pathways translates into real-world solutions for food security and energy production. Both topics appear directly in the Study Design and are assessed through extended response and application questions.

items.title: I can summarise the potential applications of CRISPR-Cas9 to improve photosynthetic efficiency and crop yields
items.what: CRISPR-Cas9 can be used to modify Rubisco activity, disable genes that promote photorespiration, increase the expression of Calvin Cycle enzymes, and potentially convert C3 crops into C4-type plants. These changes aim to reduce the energy wasted in photorespiration and increase the amount of glucose produced per unit of light energy.
items.why: With global food demand projected to roughly double by 2050, improving crop photosynthetic efficiency is a priority research area. The Study Design requires students to connect CRISPR-Cas9 mechanisms to specific photosynthesis targets.
items.example: Scientists use CRISPR-Cas9 to overexpress genes coding for enzymes that provide an alternative to the photorespiration pathway in rice plants, reducing the energy wasted and increasing grain yield by an estimated 25% in some experimental conditions.

subtopic.name: Biotechnological Applications of Biochemical Pathways
subtopic.what: Covers the use of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to improve photosynthetic efficiency and crop yields, and the use of anaerobic fermentation of biomass to produce biofuels, including the distinction between first- and second-generation biofuels and the key steps in bioethanol production.
subtopic.why: These applications show how understanding biochemical pathways translates into real-world solutions for food security and energy production. Both topics appear directly in the Study Design and are assessed through extended response and application questions.

items.title: I can define the terms biofuel and biomass
items.what: Biomass is organic material — including plant matter, animal by-products, microbes and waste — that can be used as a source of energy. A biofuel is a (usually liquid) fuel produced from biomass through biological processes such as fermentation.
items.why: These definitions are the entry point for any biofuel question. Using the precise definitions from the Study Design is required for full marks.
items.example: Corn stover (the stalks and leaves left after corn harvest) is an example of biomass. When fermented by yeast, it can be converted into bioethanol, a biofuel used to power vehicles.

subtopic.name: Biotechnological Applications of Biochemical Pathways
subtopic.what: Covers the use of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to improve photosynthetic efficiency and crop yields, and the use of anaerobic fermentation of biomass to produce biofuels, including the distinction between first- and second-generation biofuels and the key steps in bioethanol production.
subtopic.why: These applications show how understanding biochemical pathways translates into real-world solutions for food security and energy production. Both topics appear directly in the Study Design and are assessed through extended response and application questions.

items.title: I can summarise the uses and applications of anaerobic fermentation of biomass for biofuel production
items.what: Bioethanol is produced from biomass through four main steps: pre-treatment (breaking down biomass to increase surface area), enzymatic hydrolysis (using amylase or cellulase to break polysaccharides into glucose), fermentation (anaerobic conversion of glucose to ethanol and CO2 by yeast such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae) and distillation/purification (removing water to obtain usable ethanol). First-generation biofuels use edible feedstocks such as corn; second-generation biofuels use non-edible cellulose-based materials.
items.why: The production process connects enzyme theory, anaerobic respiration and sustainability concepts. The Study Design requires students to be able to describe the role of fermentation specifically within the broader production process.
items.example: In a bioethanol plant, corn starch is first pre-treated by milling, then enzymatic hydrolysis with amylase breaks the starch into glucose. Yeast ferment the glucose anaerobically (glucose → ethanol + CO2 + 2 ATP), and the ethanol is then distilled off and purified for use as fuel.
